newsitem.title: CHINA: Hong Kong court crushes challenge to constitution.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong court crushes challenge to constitution.

text.p: A Hong Kong appeals court on Tuesday crushed a challenge to the legal and constitutional arrangements that have been in place since China resumed sovereignty over the territory four weeks ago.

In a ruling favouring the post-colonial government, the court dismissed a claim that pre-handover laws had ceased to be valid, and it said it had no power to rule on the legality of the provisional legislature installed by China on July 1.
The court also ruled that a criminal conspiracy trial linked to a corruption case, from which the constitutional challenge arose, could continue.

Defence lawyers in the criminal case had argued that the British Common Law system used in Hong Kong had lapsed upon the handover of sovereignty, and that the new legislature had failed to formally adopt pre-handover laws, creating a legal vacuum.
It was the first constitutional challenge faced by the new China-backed government led by former shipping tycoon Tung Chee-hwa.
Hong Kong's post-British constitution, the Basic Law, derives its authority from China's parliament, the National People's Congress in Beijing, which promulgated it in 1990.

Hong Kong government lawyers argued that only Beijing had the power to rule on constitutional challenges, not Hong Kong courts. Solicitor General Daniel Fung, the government's victorious top lawyer, was set to meet media later in the day.
Another challenge is expected soon when lawyers representing child illegal immigrants will argue that a new law allowing their deportation back to China is a constitutional violation.
The government also faces possible constitutional challenges over its freezing of pre-handover labour rights laws.
Initial reactions from Hong Kong politicians ranged from a warm welcome from the pro-China camp to sighs of despair.
"I believe the ruling will end the quarrel over the legality of the Provisional Legislature," Allen Lee of the pro-China Liberal Party told reporters.

"I feel the court decision shows the 'one country two systems' arrangement has a legal fault which allows China's parliament to make a lot of decisions that we cannot question," said former legislator Albert Ho of the Democratic Party.

Britain handed back its former colony to China under a 1984 Sino-British treaty allowing the territory to exercise virtual autonomy in all but defence and foreign policy under China's "one country two systems" formula.
It also allows Hong Kong's distinct capitalist way of life to remain intact for a further 50 years.
